questions.question: A patient with a previously normal echocardiogram develops S. aureus bacteremia and destructive mitral IE. Which mechanism best explains why the earlier normal valve study does not exclude this diagnosis?
options: S. aureus can adhere to activated endothelium and infect valves without known structural disease
A pre-existing rheumatic lesion is required but was missed by the earlier study
Circulating immune complexes initiate every vegetation before bacteria attach
An infected venous thrombus must cross an intracardiac shunt to seed the mitral valve
questions.explanation:
Vegetation Formation and Previously Normal Valves

Correct answer: S. aureus can adhere to activated endothelium and infect valves without known structural disease

Adhesion and Growth

**Endothelial injury exposes matrix and promotes platelet–fibrin deposition.**

Microbial adhesins support attachment; organisms then proliferate within a protective vegetation.

**S. aureus also exploits activated/inflamed endothelium.**

A previously normal anatomical study does not establish resistance to infection.

Clinical Consequences

**Vegetation growth can cause destruction and embolization.**

Perforation or chordal injury causes regurgitation; extension can produce abscess or conduction disease.

**Assess current bacteremia and anatomy.**

Prior normal imaging does not replace present cultures, echocardiography or source assessment.

Endothelial injury or activation → Microbial adhesion → Platelet–fibrin vegetation growth → Destruction, extension or embolization

A pre-existing rheumatic lesion is required but was missed by the earlier study: Valve damage increases susceptibility, but S. aureus can infect previously normal valves; occult rheumatic disease is not required.

Circulating immune complexes initiate every vegetation before bacteria attach: Immune complexes help explain some extracardiac injury; they are not the obligatory initiating mechanism of bacterial valve colonization.

An infected venous thrombus must cross an intracardiac shunt to seed the mitral valve: A shunt can permit paradoxical embolism, but bloodstream bacteria can seed left-sided valves without a venous thrombus crossing a shunt.

Experimental study of S. aureus adhesion to damaged and inflamed valves — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz175

Vegetation Formation and Previously Normal Valves

Correct answer: A — S. aureus can adhere to activated endothelium and infect valves without known structural disease

Adhesion and Growth

  • Endothelial injury exposes matrix and promotes platelet–fibrin deposition.
    • Microbial adhesins support attachment; organisms then proliferate within a protective vegetation.
  • S. aureus also exploits activated/inflamed endothelium.
    • A previously normal anatomical study does not establish resistance to infection.

Clinical Consequences

  • Vegetation growth can cause destruction and embolization.
    • Perforation or chordal injury causes regurgitation; extension can produce abscess or conduction disease.
  • Assess current bacteremia and anatomy.
    • Prior normal imaging does not replace present cultures, echocardiography or source assessment.

Decision Pathway

  1. Endothelial injury or activation
  2. Microbial adhesion
  3. Platelet–fibrin vegetation growth
  4. Destruction, extension or embolization

Other Options

  • B — A pre-existing rheumatic lesion is required but was missed by the earlier study: Valve damage increases susceptibility, but S. aureus can infect previously normal valves; occult rheumatic disease is not required.
  • C — Circulating immune complexes initiate every vegetation before bacteria attach: Immune complexes help explain some extracardiac injury; they are not the obligatory initiating mechanism of bacterial valve colonization.
  • D — An infected venous thrombus must cross an intracardiac shunt to seed the mitral valve: A shunt can permit paradoxical embolism, but bloodstream bacteria can seed left-sided valves without a venous thrombus crossing a shunt.

questions.question: An adult has several weeks of fever, hematuria with red-cell casts, low complement and a splenic wedge-shaped infarct. Two separately collected blood-culture sets grow Streptococcus mitis. No murmur is heard. Which diagnosis best unifies the findings?
options: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis
Left-sided infective endocarditis
Lupus-associated Libman–Sacks endocarditis
Malignancy-associated nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis
questions.explanation:
Endocarditis Without a Detectable Murmur

Correct answer: Left-sided infective endocarditis

Systemic Presentation

**IE can occur without an audible murmur.**

Typical-organism bacteremia, systemic embolism and immune-complex renal injury form a coherent presentation.

**Renal injury:** casts and low complement suggest glomerulonephritis.

Renal arterial embolism is a different mechanism; both may coexist.

Diagnostic and Treatment Sequence

**Cultures → TTE → TEE when indicated.**

Assess vegetation, regurgitation, ventricular function and periannular extension.

**Treat the organism and assess surgical indications.**

Heart failure, uncontrolled infection and embolic risk drive escalation; exclude infection before immunosuppression for presumed vasculitis.

ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis: Vasculitis can cause fever and glomerular injury, but the concordant typical-organism bacteremia and embolic lesion make an endovascular infection a more coherent explanation. Infection can also generate misleading immune-test abnormalities.

Lupus-associated Libman–Sacks endocarditis: Sterile valve lesions can occur with lupus and accompany nephritis or emboli. The repeated typical-organism cultures instead require active investigation for infectious endocarditis rather than assuming a sterile immune process.

Malignancy-associated nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis: NBTE can cause systemic emboli and may occur without a prominent murmur. It does not best explain repeated oral-streptococcal bacteremia with an inflammatory renal syndrome; malignancy and infection are not distinguished by the murmur alone.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: A stable antibiotic-naive adult has a subacute illness strongly suspicious for IE, without shock or another need for immediate resuscitation. Which collection plan best follows ESC 2023 practice?
options: Obtain the sets only when the temperature next reaches its peak
Obtain one peripheral set and begin treatment once it flags positive
Obtain three adequately filled peripheral culture sets before starting antibiotics
Begin empirical antibiotics and collect three sets after the first dose
questions.explanation:
Pre-Antibiotic Blood Cultures in a Stable Suspected Case

Correct answer: Obtain three adequately filled peripheral culture sets before starting antibiotics

Stable Pre-Treatment Sampling

**At least three peripheral sets before antibiotics** under ESC 2023.

Collect at roughly ==30-minute== intervals using aseptic technique; each set usually contains aerobic and anaerobic bottles.

Fill adult bottles according to the system, commonly ==8–10 mL== each.

**Continuous bacteremia:** do not wait for a fever spike.

Sampling Versus Classification

**Duke–ISCVID 2023:** a typical organism in ≥2 separate sets can meet the microbiological major criterion.

Two bottles from one set are not two sets; classification thresholds do not replace adequate clinical sampling.

**Deterioration changes timing.**

Collect promptly and treat immediately in shock; the stable timetable must not delay antibiotics.

Obtain the sets only when the temperature next reaches its peak: Timing at a fever peak is useful for some historical sampling assumptions, but IE commonly produces continuous bacteremia. Waiting for a spike can delay useful specimens without improving the diagnostic strategy.

Obtain one peripheral set and begin treatment once it flags positive: One set can detect bacteremia, but provides less sensitivity and less ability to distinguish contamination from sustained infection. The stable suspected-IE presentation permits an adequate pre-treatment collection rather than relying on a single specimen.

Begin empirical antibiotics and collect three sets after the first dose: Treatment before collection can be necessary when delay would compromise an unstable patient. The supplied stable untreated presentation allows cultures first and avoids preventable antibiotic-suppressed culture-negative disease.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

AHA blood culture-negative endocarditis scientific statement, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.124.040218

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic valve has probable endovascular infection, hypotension, altered mentation and rising lactate. Cultures can be collected immediately, but completing the usual spaced stable-patient collection would postpone antibiotics. Which sequence is most appropriate?
options: Complete the full spaced sampling sequence before administering antibiotics
Collect cultures promptly and start appropriate empirical IV therapy immediately while resuscitating
Obtain TEE confirmation before choosing whether to start antimicrobial treatment
Wait for an initial culture Gram stain before selecting empirical therapy
questions.explanation:
Blood Cultures and Antibiotic Timing in Septic Shock

Correct answer: Collect cultures promptly and start appropriate empirical IV therapy immediately while resuscitating

Immediate Shock Response

**Prompt cultures → immediate empirical IV therapy plus resuscitation.**

SSC 2026 targets treatment ideally within ==1 hour== for septic shock; do not wait for spaced sampling, TEE or culture growth.

Source and Organ Support

**Choose coverage by valve setting, acquisition, resistance risk and organ function.**

Early prosthetic and healthcare-associated infection require broader assessment than uncomplicated community-acquired disease.

**Urgent echo and multidisciplinary source control.**

Assess valve failure, abscess and dehiscence; involve surgery when indicated.

**Monitor perfusion, renal function, lactate and cultures.**

Individualize fluids and vasoactive support to cardiac physiology; narrow antibiotics after reliable microbiology.

Complete the full spaced sampling sequence before administering antibiotics: A spaced collection is appropriate in a stable suspected case. It must not delay time-critical treatment of probable infection with shock; prompt feasible sampling and treatment take priority.

Obtain TEE confirmation before choosing whether to start antimicrobial treatment: TEE is important for locating prosthetic-valve infection and complications. A patient with probable infectious shock requires immediate treatment and stabilization while the imaging pathway proceeds.

Wait for an initial culture Gram stain before selecting empirical therapy: A rapid Gram stain can refine treatment when available, but waiting for culture growth in shock delays effective coverage. Start a context-appropriate empirical regimen and revise it as microbiology becomes available.

Surviving Sepsis Campaign adult guidelines, 2026 — https://www.sccm.org/clinical-resources/guidelines/guidelines/surviving-sepsis-campaign-international-guidelines-for-management-of-sepsis-and-septic-shock-2026

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

AHA blood culture-negative endocarditis scientific statement, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.124.040218

questions.question: A patient receiving active treatment for MSSA bacteremia has repeat positive cultures after 72 hours. A technically limited TTE shows no vegetation. The patient has new back pain. Which next plan is most appropriate?
options: Change to vancomycin and reassess imaging after cultures clear
Repeat TTE after a further two weeks of treatment
Investigate endovascular infection with TEE and search for a metastatic or uncontrolled focus
Obtain spinal MRI and manage an isolated vertebral infection
questions.explanation:
Persistent Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia

Correct answer: Investigate endovascular infection with TEE and search for a metastatic or uncontrolled focus

Persistent MSSA Bacteremia

**Positive cultures at 72 hours demand source reassessment.**

Confirm active drug, dose and delivery; review vascular access and implanted material.

**Repeat cultures until clearance.**

A falling CRP cannot establish microbiological cure.

Localize the Sustaining Focus

**TEE after a limited TTE; investigate new focal back pain.**

Vertebral infection can coexist with IE; spinal MRI does not replace cardiac assessment.

**Drain or remove an uncontrolled focus when indicated.**

Persistence at 72 hours is not automatically a formal surgical-persistence threshold; valve findings and complications determine treatment duration and escalation.

Change to vancomycin and reassess imaging after cultures clear: Vancomycin is important when MRSA or a relevant beta-lactam limitation is present. Persistence of a susceptible MSSA episode can reflect an uncontrolled focus, so changing drugs while postponing source investigation is less appropriate.

Repeat TTE after a further two weeks of treatment: Interval TTE can be useful for response assessment in a stable adequately characterized episode. Persistent MSSA bacteremia with a limited initial study and new focal pain needs earlier, more complete assessment rather than that delayed plan.

Obtain spinal MRI and manage an isolated vertebral infection: Vertebral infection is a relevant concern and needs directed investigation. It can coexist with IE, so finding or suspecting a spinal focus does not justify an isolated-spine diagnosis without cardiac-source assessment.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

AHA blood culture-negative endocarditis scientific statement, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.124.040218

questions.question: With no pathological confirmation available, which combination meets the clinical definition of definite infective endocarditis in the 2023 Duke–ISCVID criteria?
options: One major criterion and two minor criteria
One major criterion and three minor criteria
Four minor criteria without a major criterion
One major criterion without a minor criterion
questions.explanation:
Clinical Classification With Duke–ISCVID Criteria

Correct answer: One major criterion and three minor criteria

Apply the Clinical Combinations

**Definite:** 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor.

If not definite, 1 major + 1–2 minor or 3–4 minor supports possible IE.

**Count categories, not repeated observations.**

More positive cultures within one microbiological category do not create additional major criteria.

Pathology and Clinical Judgment

**Qualifying tissue evidence can establish pathological definite IE.**

Interpret organism detection and active-endocarditis histology with prior treatment and contamination risk.

**Classification does not determine treatment by itself.**

Early disease can be underclassified; assess organism, anatomy, complications and competing diagnoses without delaying necessary therapy.

Duke–ISCVID component | Qualifying combination or evidence

Clinical definite | 2 major; or 1 major + 3 minor; or 5 minor

Possible, if not definite | 1 major + 1–2 minor; or 3–4 minor

Microbiological major | Typical organism in ≥2 sets; nontypical organism in ≥3 sets; or specified organism-specific blood molecular/serological evidence

Imaging major | Qualifying echo/CT lesion such as vegetation, abscess or fistula; significant new regurgitation on echo; new prosthetic dehiscence; or qualifying FDG uptake

Surgical major | Direct operative evidence when qualifying imaging and subsequent histological/microbiological confirmation are absent

Minor: predisposition | Qualifying valve disease, prosthetic or repair material, previous IE, CHD, CIED, HOCM or injection drug use

Minor: fever | Documented temperature ==>38°C==

Minor: vascular | Arterial embolus, septic pulmonary infarct, cerebral/splenic abscess, infective aneurysm, intracranial or conjunctival hemorrhage, Janeway lesions or purulent purpura

Minor: immunological | Rheumatoid factor, Osler nodes, Roth spots or qualifying immune-complex glomerulonephritis

Minor: microbiological | Compatible evidence short of major, with the specified contaminant exclusions

Minor: imaging | Qualifying early prosthetic FDG uptake within 3 months

Minor: physical examination | New regurgitant murmur only if echocardiography is unavailable; a changing pre-existing murmur is insufficient

Pathological route | Separate qualifying organism or active-endocarditis tissue evidence in the appropriate clinical context

One major criterion and two minor criteria: This combination reaches possible IE but does not reach the clinical definite threshold. It can still justify urgent investigation and treatment when the overall clinical probability is high.

Four minor criteria without a major criterion: Three or four minor criteria can support possible IE. Five minor criteria are required for the clinical definite route when there is no major criterion.

One major criterion without a minor criterion: A major finding demands clinical evaluation, but a single major criterion alone does not meet the clinical possible or definite combinations. A separate qualifying pathological finding would use a different route.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

Minor: feverDocumented temperature >38°C
Minor: vascularArterial embolus, septic pulmonary infarct, cerebral/splenic abscess, infective aneurysm, intracranial or conjunctival hemorrhage, Janeway lesions or purulent purpura
Minor: immunologicalRheumatoid factor, Osler nodes, Roth spots or qualifying immune-complex glomerulonephritis
Minor: microbiologicalCompatible evidence short of major, with the specified contaminant exclusions
Minor: imagingQualifying early prosthetic FDG uptake within 3 months
Minor: physical examinationNew regurgitant murmur only if echocardiography is unavailable; a changing pre-existing murmur is insufficient
Pathological routeSeparate qualifying organism or active-endocarditis tissue evidence in the appropriate clinical context

Other Options

  • One major criterion and two minor criteria: This combination reaches possible IE but does not reach the clinical definite threshold. It can still justify urgent investigation and treatment when the overall clinical probability is high.
  • Four minor criteria without a major criterion: Three or four minor criteria can support possible IE. Five minor criteria are required for the clinical definite route when there is no major criterion.
  • One major criterion without a minor criterion: A major finding demands clinical evaluation, but a single major criterion alone does not meet the clinical possible or definite combinations. A separate qualifying pathological finding would use a different route.

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic valve has fever of 38.6°C and Enterococcus faecalis in two separate blood-culture sets. Initial cardiac imaging provides no major imaging finding. No other criteria are present. Which additional finding would establish clinically definite IE under Duke–ISCVID 2023?
options: Newly documented splenomegaly without an embolic lesion
A third culture set growing the same E. faecalis
A further rise in serum C-reactive protein
An imaging-confirmed new splenic arterial embolus
questions.explanation:
Adding a Distinct Criterion Rather Than Recounting Cultures

Correct answer: An imaging-confirmed new splenic arterial embolus

Count the Existing Evidence

**Starting score: one major + two minor.**

Two E. faecalis culture sets provide microbiological major evidence; prosthetic valve and fever >38°C are separate minor domains.

Add a Distinct Domain

**Splenic arterial embolus adds vascular minor evidence.**

The total becomes one major + three minor: clinically definite IE.

**Repeated findings do not multiply domains.**

Multiple emboli remain one vascular domain; repeated fever remains one fever domain.

Another concordant culture supports persistence but does not create a second microbiological major criterion.

**Continue anatomical assessment** after reaching definite classification.

Newly documented splenomegaly without an embolic lesion: Splenomegaly can accompany a prolonged infection and deserves investigation. Enlargement alone is not equivalent to a vascular embolus and does not independently fulfill the vascular minor criterion.

A third culture set growing the same E. faecalis: Additional concordant cultures strengthen evidence of sustained bacteremia and guide clearance assessment. The existing typical-organism cultures already satisfy the microbiological major category, so another set does not create a second major criterion.

A further rise in serum C-reactive protein: CRP can support assessment of inflammation and its trajectory during treatment. It is nonspecific and is not an additional Duke–ISCVID minor criterion, so its rise does not supply the missing category.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: During evaluation for IE, a patient has tender fingertip nodules and painless erythematous macules on the soles. Which classification of these findings matches Duke–ISCVID 2023?
options: Osler nodes are vascular phenomena; Janeway lesions are immunological phenomena
Osler nodes are immunological phenomena; Janeway lesions are vascular phenomena
Both findings count separately within the immunological domain
Both findings count separately within the vascular domain
questions.explanation:
Peripheral Signs and Their Diagnostic Domains

Correct answer: Osler nodes are immunological phenomena; Janeway lesions are vascular phenomena

Recognize the Findings

**Osler nodes:** tender fingertip/toe-pad nodules.

Count as immunological evidence alongside Roth spots, rheumatoid factor or qualifying immune-complex GN.

**Janeway lesions:** painless hemorrhagic/erythematous palm or sole lesions.

Count as vascular evidence, as do qualifying embolic manifestations.

Avoid Overclassification

**Roth spots are pale-centered retinal hemorrhages; splinter hemorrhages are subungual.**

Both have other causes; isolated splinter hemorrhages are not a listed standalone Duke minor criterion.

**Clinical signs support, but do not replace, microbiology and imaging.**

Count each applicable domain once and interpret the whole illness.

Osler nodes are vascular phenomena; Janeway lesions are immunological phenomena: This reverses their diagnostic categories; tenderness helps identify Osler nodes, whereas painless palm/sole lesions suggest Janeway lesions.

Both findings count separately within the immunological domain: Osler nodes belong to that domain, but Janeway lesions are vascular; multiple findings within one domain are not separate minor criteria.

Both findings count separately within the vascular domain: Janeway lesions are vascular, but Osler nodes are immunological; the criteria count domains rather than each individual skin lesion.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: An older adult develops E. faecalis bacteremia after urinary instrumentation. Two separate blood-culture sets are positive. No prosthetic valve is present. Under Duke–ISCVID 2023, how should this microbiology be classified?
options: A major criterion only if intracardiac prosthetic material is present
A microbiological minor criterion because the source is urinary
A major criterion only if a third culture set is positive
A microbiological major criterion despite the apparent urinary source
questions.explanation:
Enterococcus faecalis Bacteremia With a Urinary Source

Correct answer: A microbiological major criterion despite the apparent urinary source

Typical Organism Rule

**E. faecalis is typical irrespective of acquisition or primary source.**

Two separate positive sets satisfy the microbiological major threshold; a urinary source does not remove that designation.

**Do not extrapolate to every enterococcal species.**

Identification and the named framework determine the culture threshold.

Interpret the Whole Episode

**One major criterion alone does not establish definite IE.**

Integrate fever, predisposition, embolic or immune findings and appropriate cardiac imaging.

**Treat and investigate the urinary source while assessing endovascular seeding.**

Document clearance; a primary source and valve infection can coexist. A major criterion alone does not mandate a full IE regimen.

A major criterion only if intracardiac prosthetic material is present: Intracardiac material expands the list of typical organisms to include selected additional pathogens. E. faecalis is already typical without that context and does not require a prosthesis to meet the culture definition.

A microbiological minor criterion because the source is urinary: A positive culture that falls short of a major definition may contribute a microbiological minor criterion. E. faecalis in the stated number of sets meets the revised typical-organism major definition even when a primary source is identified.

A major criterion only if a third culture set is positive: Three or more separate positive sets are the culture threshold for organisms that only occasionally or rarely cause IE. E. faecalis is in the typical group, for which two separate positive sets suffice.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic aortic valve has persistent fever and Cutibacterium acnes growing in two separately collected blood-culture sets. Under Duke–ISCVID 2023, which interpretation best fits these findings?
options: The cultures qualify only as minor evidence until a third set is positive
The prosthetic context allows the cultures to meet a microbiological major criterion
The cultures meet a pathological criterion without a valve specimen
The cultures establish clinically definite IE without further criteria
questions.explanation:
Typical Pathogens in the Presence of a Prosthesis

Correct answer: The prosthetic context allows the cultures to meet a microbiological major criterion

Prosthesis-Dependent Microbiology

**Intracardiac prosthetic material expands the typical-organism list.**

C. acnes in two separate sets qualifies here; the comparison table lists other context-dependent organisms.

**Retain contamination awareness.**

One poorly collected positive specimen in a well patient is a different scenario.

Define Prosthetic Involvement

**TEE assesses prosthetic function and local infection.**

CT or metabolic imaging can clarify inconclusive periannular findings.

**Blood evidence remains a clinical major criterion.**

It is neither pathological confirmation nor a complete definite-IE combination by itself.

Obtain susceptibility testing and operative tissue when available; assess invasion, persistent infection and source control.

Additional typical group with intracardiac prosthetic material | Examples

Skin-associated organisms | Coagulase-negative staphylococci; C. acnes; C. striatum; C. jeikeium

Selected Gram-negative organisms | S. marcescens; P. aeruginosa

Other implant-associated pathogens | Nontuberculous mycobacteria, especially M. chimaera; Candida species

The cultures qualify only as minor evidence until a third set is positive: That higher culture threshold applies to nontypical organisms. C. acnes belongs to the additional typical group when intracardiac prosthetic material is present, so the stated two-set evidence meets the major definition.

The cultures meet a pathological criterion without a valve specimen: Pathological confirmation uses qualifying tissue or embolic material in its appropriate clinical context. Blood cultures provide microbiological clinical evidence; they are not transformed into tissue confirmation by the presence of a prosthesis.

The cultures establish clinically definite IE without further criteria: Repeated concordant cultures are concerning and warrant investigation, particularly with a prosthesis. They provide one major category rather than the two major or other qualifying combinations needed for clinical definite classification.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: In a patient being assessed for culture-negative endocarditis, which blood test is explicitly sufficient for a microbiological major criterion under Duke–ISCVID 2023?
options: A Coxiella phase-II IgG titre of 1:1600 in isolation
A validated blood PCR positive for Tropheryma whipplei
A Bartonella henselae IgG titre of 1:128 in isolation
A single blood-culture bottle growing Staphylococcus epidermidis
questions.explanation:
Blood Molecular Evidence in Culture-Negative Endocarditis

Correct answer: A validated blood PCR positive for Tropheryma whipplei

Blood Molecular Major Criterion

**Qualifying blood nucleic-acid evidence:** C. burnetii, Bartonella spp. or T. whipplei.

A validated T. whipplei PCR fits; an arbitrary positive molecular test does not.

**One major criterion still requires clinical integration.**

Assess assay validity, phenotype, imaging and alternative sources of the signal.

Serology and Tissue

**Use organism- and method-specific thresholds** shown in the table.

Coxiella phase-II antibodies cannot replace the phase-I criterion.

**Plan tissue allocation before fixation.**

Coordinate culture, histology and molecular testing; DNA may persist after successful treatment.

**Prior antibiotics commonly explain negative cultures.**

Do not assume every culture-negative episode is a fastidious infection.

Qualifying result in Duke–ISCVID 2023 | Major threshold

Blood nucleic-acid test | C. burnetii, Bartonella spp. or T. whipplei

C. burnetii serology | Phase-I IgG ==>1:800==, or equivalent method-specific result

B. henselae or B. quintana serology | IgG ==≥1:800== by the specified immunofluorescence approach, or equivalent result

A Coxiella phase-II IgG titre of 1:1600 in isolation: Phase-II antibodies are useful in evaluating Q fever, particularly acute infection. The specified IE serological major criterion uses phase-I IgG above its threshold; a high isolated phase-II titre cannot be substituted for it.

A Bartonella henselae IgG titre of 1:128 in isolation: Bartonella serology is appropriate in a compatible culture-negative presentation. This result does not reach the specified IgG major threshold of at least 1:800, and lower titres require contextual interpretation and potentially further testing.

A single blood-culture bottle growing Staphylococcus epidermidis: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are important in prosthetic infection, but one isolated positive bottle can also represent contamination. It does not supply the stated repeated-set major evidence, and the organism-specific single-culture exception for Coxiella cannot be applied to it.

questions.question: Six weeks after valve replacement, a patient with suspected PVE has intense focal periprosthetic FDG uptake on a technically adequate study interpreted by an experienced team. How do the published 2023 Duke–ISCVID and ESC diagnostic frameworks treat this finding?
options: Duke–ISCVID counts early uptake as major; ESC restricts it to minor
Both frameworks require waiting three months before the finding can contribute
Both frameworks classify any postoperative FDG uptake as major
Duke–ISCVID counts early uptake as minor; ESC can count the characteristic pattern as major
questions.explanation:
Early Prosthetic-Valve FDG Uptake: Name the Framework

Correct answer: Duke–ISCVID counts early uptake as minor; ESC can count the characteristic pattern as major

Name the 2023 Framework

**Duke–ISCVID:** qualifying prosthetic FDG uptake within 3 months is minor.

Its prosthetic major definition uses the specified pattern at least 3 months after surgical implantation.

**ESC:** intense focal or heterogeneous prosthetic/periprosthetic uptake can be major irrespective of surgical interval.

Avoid False-Positive Interpretation

**Postoperative inflammation can mimic infection.**

Review preparation, attenuation artifacts, surgical material and uptake distribution with imaging expertise.

**Integrate TEE, CT, microbiology and clinical course.**

Neither framework makes every postoperative uptake pattern infectious; do not create an unnamed hybrid of their criteria.

Duke–ISCVID counts early uptake as major; ESC restricts it to minor: This reverses the relevant distinction. The 2023 ESC approach permits qualifying prosthetic uptake as a major finding without a fixed postoperative interval, whereas the Duke–ISCVID framework retains an early-period minor designation.

Both frameworks require waiting three months before the finding can contribute: A waiting threshold can reduce confusion from postoperative inflammation, but neither named framework simply discards all early uptake. Duke–ISCVID includes early uptake as minor, while ESC uses the characteristic pattern irrespective of the surgical interval.

Both frameworks classify any postoperative FDG uptake as major: Metabolic activity can reflect healing or other noninfectious processes. Pattern, location, preparation and expert interpretation matter; the statement also overlooks the Duke–ISCVID early-implant minor category.

  • Duke–ISCVID: qualifying prosthetic FDG uptake within 3 months is minor.

questions.question: During valve surgery, the surgeon documents vegetation and destructive infection. Preoperative imaging did not meet a major criterion, and subsequent histology and microbiology do not provide confirmation. What role can the operative observation have under Duke–ISCVID 2023?
options: It can provide the surgical major clinical criterion in this specified setting
It independently constitutes pathological definite IE without tissue confirmation
It contributes only a vascular minor criterion because it was observed directly
It cannot contribute unless the valve culture is positive
questions.explanation:
Direct Surgical Inspection and Pathological Confirmation

Correct answer: It can provide the surgical major clinical criterion in this specified setting

Conditional Surgical Major Criterion

**Direct operative IE evidence can provide a clinical major criterion** when qualifying imaging and subsequent tissue confirmation are absent.

Document vegetation, abscess, destruction or infected prosthetic dehiscence precisely.

**Do not count the same anatomical evidence repeatedly.**

Preserve Tissue Diagnosis

**Macroscopic inspection is not pathological confirmation.**

Send specimens for microbiology, histology and selected molecular testing.

**Negative culture does not prove sterility**, especially after antibiotics.

Conversely, a nonspecific mass is not automatically infectious.

**One surgical major alone does not establish clinical definite IE.**

Apply the remaining criteria or the separate pathological route if qualifying tissue evidence becomes available.

It independently constitutes pathological definite IE without tissue confirmation: Qualifying tissue microbiology or active-endocarditis histology can establish the pathological route. A surgeon’s direct macroscopic observation is instead assigned a specific clinical major role when the stated other confirmation is unavailable.

It contributes only a vascular minor criterion because it was observed directly: Vascular minor evidence concerns embolic and other specified vascular manifestations. Directly observed valve destruction or vegetation is evidence at the cardiac source and belongs to the separate surgical major provision.

It cannot contribute unless the valve culture is positive: Positive tissue microbiology would be valuable and should be sought. Its absence does not automatically erase a well-documented operative finding, particularly after antibiotics; the revised surgical major provision addresses this diagnostic gap.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic mitral valve has persistent fever and repeatedly positive cultures for a typical IE organism. TTE does not adequately visualize the sewing ring and reports no definite vegetation. Which cardiac investigation is the most appropriate next step?
options: Transesophageal echocardiography
Repeat transthoracic echocardiography as the sole next study
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging
ECG-gated cardiac CT
questions.explanation:
Prosthetic-Valve Infection After a Nondiagnostic TTE

Correct answer: Transesophageal echocardiography

Next Test: TEE

**High suspicion plus nondiagnostic prosthetic TTE warrants TEE.**

Acoustic shadowing can conceal sewing-ring infection; no visible vegetation is not equivalent to exclusion.

**TTE remains complementary** for ventricular function and hemodynamics.

Assess Extension

**Look beyond vegetation:** regurgitation, dehiscence, abscess, pseudoaneurysm and fistula.

ESC 2023 generally also recommends TEE after positive TTE; isolated right-sided native IE with conclusive high-quality TTE is an exception.

**Inconclusive or infeasible TEE:** select CT or nuclear imaging for the unresolved question.

Urgent treatment and source-control assessment proceed alongside imaging.

Repeat transthoracic echocardiography as the sole next study: Repeat TTE is useful for changing hemodynamics or interval assessment and may provide better images in some circumstances. Here the known prosthetic limitation and high suspicion make TEE the appropriate next anatomical examination rather than another transthoracic study alone.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging: CMR can characterize ventricular function and other myocardial disease. For suspected prosthetic vegetation and sewing-ring complications, its spatial and artifact limitations make it less suitable than TEE as the immediate next test.

ECG-gated cardiac CT: Cardiac CT is useful for periprosthetic extension, particularly when TEE is inconclusive or not feasible. With no supplied TEE contraindication, the next standard examination is TEE to assess the prosthesis, dynamic valve function and adjacent structures.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A clinically stable patient has persistent typical-organism bacteremia and a high clinical suspicion of IE. Initial TTE and TEE are negative, with no new shock, HF or conduction change. Which follow-up imaging plan best follows ESC 2023?
options: Replace repeat echocardiography with a negative native-valve FDG-PET study
Repeat echocardiography only at the end of the antibiotic course
Repeat echocardiography only if a new murmur becomes audible
Repeat echocardiography in approximately five to seven days while continuing the investigation
questions.explanation:
Repeat Imaging After an Initially Negative Examination

Correct answer: Repeat echocardiography in approximately five to seven days while continuing the investigation

Repeat Echocardiography

**ESC 2023: repeat after approximately 5–7 days** if initial imaging is normal/inconclusive and suspicion remains high.

Early or small lesions may initially escape detection.

**Deterioration requires earlier reassessment.**

New HF, embolism or conduction change overrides the planned interval.

Active Investigation During the Interval

**Follow cultures, susceptibility and extracardiac sources.**

Choose repeat TTE/TEE and complementary imaging according to the suspected structure and prior limitations.

**A negative native-valve PET cannot exclude IE.**

Limited sensitivity prevents it from replacing indicated repeat echo; neither waiting for a murmur nor end-of-course imaging addresses current persistent suspicion.

Replace repeat echocardiography with a negative native-valve FDG-PET study: PET can add selected diagnostic or extracardiac information. Its limited native-valve sensitivity means that a negative scan cannot substitute for an appropriate repeat echocardiographic assessment.

Repeat echocardiography only at the end of the antibiotic course: End-of-treatment imaging can provide a useful reference after a diagnosed episode. It is too late to resolve persistent high diagnostic suspicion or detect an evolving lesion during the current illness.

Repeat echocardiography only if a new murmur becomes audible: A new murmur can prompt reassessment but is not a prerequisite for repeat imaging. Persistent high suspicion and bacteremia justify follow-up even before an audible valve abnormality develops.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: A patient with aortic-valve IE develops new PR prolongation. TEE suggests a periannular abnormality but cannot define its extent because of prosthetic artifact. The patient is stable enough for additional imaging. Which test best clarifies the suspected local complication?
options: FDG-PET/CT without a dedicated cardiac angiographic acquisition
Repeat TEE after a further five to seven days
ECG-gated contrast-enhanced cardiac CT
Contrast-enhanced cardiac MRI
questions.explanation:
Cardiac CT for Suspected Aortic Root Extension

Correct answer: ECG-gated contrast-enhanced cardiac CT

Conduction Change and Root Extension

**New PR prolongation or AV block in aortic IE suggests periannular invasion.**

The conduction system lies near the aortic annulus; prompt Endocarditis Team assessment is required.

Map the Anatomy

**ECG-gated contrast cardiac CT** clarifies extension hidden by prosthetic artifact.

Abscess: infected collection; pseudoaneurysm: cavity communicating with the lumen; fistula: abnormal connection between structures.

**CT and TEE are complementary.**

CT maps perivalvular anatomy; TEE better depicts small mobile vegetations and dynamic valve findings.

**Review renal function, contrast risk and acquisition quality.**

Imaging must not postpone necessary urgent source control.

FDG-PET/CT without a dedicated cardiac angiographic acquisition: PET can support the presence of prosthetic infection and find distant foci. The immediate unresolved question is the detailed periannular cavity anatomy; dedicated gated contrast CT is better suited to map that anatomy for intervention.

Repeat TEE after a further five to seven days: Repeat echocardiography is appropriate for initially occult lesions when suspicion remains high. A new conduction abnormality with a suspected periannular lesion requires prompt definition of extension rather than waiting for routine interval reassessment.

Contrast-enhanced cardiac MRI: CMR can assess myocardial tissue and ventricular function in selected cases. It is less suited than gated cardiac CT to the small periannular structures and prosthetic artifact problem that must be resolved here.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic aortic valve implanted two years ago has ongoing clinical suspicion of PVE. TEE and cardiac CT remain inconclusive. Which additional study best complements these examinations and evaluates possible distant infection?
options: Properly prepared whole-body FDG-PET/CT
Another TEE as the sole additional study
Contrast CT limited to the abdomen and pelvis
Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement
questions.explanation:
Metabolic Imaging After Inconclusive Prosthetic Studies

Correct answer: Properly prepared whole-body FDG-PET/CT

Prosthetic and Whole-Body Assessment

**FDG-PET/CT adds metabolic evidence** after inconclusive anatomical studies.

Prepare to suppress physiological myocardial uptake; review artifacts and noninfectious inflammation.

**Whole-body imaging can reveal metastatic foci or a portal of entry.**

Brain lesions may still need CT/MRI because physiological cerebral uptake limits PET.

Interpretation Limits

**Characteristic uptake supports infection; negative imaging does not universally exclude it.**

Sensitivity differs for native valves, prostheses, pockets and leads.

**Pocket-only uptake does not prove intracardiac lead infection.**

Integrate the precise location, pattern, cultures and valve function; late postoperative uptake is not automatically infectious.

Another TEE as the sole additional study: Serial TEE can reveal evolving valve lesions and reassess function. After inconclusive anatomical studies, it does not provide the additional metabolic evidence or whole-body infection survey requested in this stem.

Contrast CT limited to the abdomen and pelvis: Abdominal CT can define splenic, renal and other local complications or possible sources. A scan limited to those regions does not investigate the unresolved prosthetic metabolic signal, although targeted CT may follow a focus detected by another method.

Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement: CMR is valuable for myocardial characterization in selected cardiac disorders. It is less established for prosthetic infection and does not offer the requested prosthetic metabolic assessment with a systemic focus survey.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient with confirmed IE develops focal lumbar pain, vertebral percussion tenderness and rising inflammatory markers despite improving valve hemodynamics. There is no contraindication to MRI. Which study best assesses the suspected metastatic spinal complication?
options: Repeat TEE as the only additional investigation
Plain lumbar radiographs as the definitive exclusion test
MRI of the symptomatic spine with an appropriate infection protocol
CT of the lumbar spine without further imaging if normal
questions.explanation:
Imaging a Suspected Metastatic Spinal Focus

Correct answer: MRI of the symptomatic spine with an appropriate infection protocol

Investigate the Spinal Focus

**New focal back pain in IE suggests spondylodiscitis or associated collection.**

Check weakness, sensory loss, saddle symptoms and sphincter dysfunction; neurological compromise requires urgent specialist assessment.

MRI and Source Control

**MRI defines marrow, disc, epidural and paravertebral involvement.**

Choose the infection protocol and contrast use with radiology; degeneration and malignancy can mimic findings.

**Collection, instability or compression can require intervention.**

Consider sampling when the organism is uncertain or response is discordant.

**Treat the complete infection.**

A spinal focus may alter duration; improving valve function does not establish metastatic source control or remove a valve-surgery indication.

Repeat TEE as the only additional investigation: Repeat TEE is appropriate if valve dysfunction or local progression is suspected. It does not characterize a painful spinal focus, and improving hemodynamics does not exclude metastatic infection.

Plain lumbar radiographs as the definitive exclusion test: Radiographs can show established destructive changes or another structural cause of pain. Early spondylodiscitis or an epidural collection can be missed, so normal films cannot provide the requested exclusion.

CT of the lumbar spine without further imaging if normal: CT can show bone destruction and is useful when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated. MRI better assesses early disc, marrow and epidural or paravertebral involvement in this compatible presentation.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma has recurrent systemic emboli and a mitral-valve mass. There is no fever or inflammatory syndrome. Multiple adequately collected pre-antibiotic cultures and a directed fastidious-organism evaluation are negative. Which diagnosis should now be strongly considered?
options: Antibiotic-suppressed bacterial endocarditis
Malignancy-associated nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis
Lupus-associated Libman–Sacks endocarditis
Papillary fibroelastoma
questions.explanation:
A Valve Mass in a Patient With Cancer

Correct answer: Malignancy-associated nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis

Malignancy-Associated NBTE

**Sterile thrombotic valve deposits** occur with advanced malignancy and hypercoagulability.

Systemic emboli may dominate while valve dysfunction is limited; a mass alone does not establish IE.

**TEE characterizes morphology but cannot reliably determine every lesion’s cause.**

Exclude Infection and Select Treatment

**Review pre-antibiotic cultures and directed fastidious testing.**

Typical bacteremia, fever, valve destruction or abscess would renew concern for IE.

**Treat the underlying cancer and assess anticoagulation individually.**

Consider bleeding and cerebral lesions; this differs from anticoagulation solely to prevent septic emboli in IE.

**Reassess contradictory evidence.**

Lupus/APS lesions and fibroelastoma remain context-dependent alternatives.

Antibiotic-suppressed bacterial endocarditis: Antibiotic exposure before sampling is a common reason for negative cultures in true IE. The stem specifies adequate pre-antibiotic sampling, making that explanation less persuasive while the malignancy-associated thrombotic phenotype is prominent.

Lupus-associated Libman–Sacks endocarditis: Sterile valve lesions can occur with lupus or antiphospholipid disease and cause emboli. No autoimmune phenotype is supplied, whereas advanced pancreatic malignancy provides a strong alternative substrate.

Papillary fibroelastoma: A valvular fibroelastoma can appear as a mobile mass and can embolize, so it remains an imaging differential. The systemic thrombotic cancer context and overall assessment make NBTE the stronger unifying consideration; morphology and tissue evidence can refine uncertainty.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.topic: Blood culture-negative disease and organism clues
questions.question: A patient received several days of antibiotics before referral. TEE now shows a destructive valve lesion, but all blood cultures collected after treatment are negative. Which interpretation should guide the initial culture-negative assessment?
options: The negative cultures preferentially establish a fungal cause
Negative cultures make a nonbacterial thrombotic lesion the leading explanation
Common IE bacteria may have been suppressed by prior treatment
The negative cultures justify limiting treatment to fastidious intracellular organisms
questions.explanation:
Culture Negativity After Empirical Antibiotics

Correct answer: Common IE bacteria may have been suppressed by prior treatment

Interpret the Antibiotic History

**Prior antibiotics can suppress ordinary IE bacteria.**

Retrieve agents, doses, timing and pre-treatment cultures; negative treated samples differ from adequately sampled untreated blood.

**Untreated culture-negative disease** warrants organism-directed investigation guided by exposures and valve setting.

Refine Diagnosis and Treatment

**No single empirical BCNE regimen fits every patient.**

Consider acquisition, valve type, resistance risk, previous treatment and organ function.

**Coordinate cultures, targeted serology/PCR and operative tissue testing.**

Do not interrupt necessary treatment in unstable or complicated disease merely to improve yield.

**Review sterile mimics when the phenotype warrants**, not solely because treated cultures are negative.

The negative cultures preferentially establish a fungal cause: Fungal IE can be difficult to diagnose and requires consideration with relevant risk factors. Post-treatment culture negativity is not specific for fungi and commonly reflects suppression of ordinary bacteria.

Negative cultures make a nonbacterial thrombotic lesion the leading explanation: NBTE is an important differential when the clinical context suggests a sterile thrombotic process. Cultures collected after antibiotics lose sensitivity, so their negativity cannot by itself override a destructive infectious phenotype.

The negative cultures justify limiting treatment to fastidious intracellular organisms: Fastidious infection deserves a directed investigation, especially without prior antibiotics. Here antibiotic exposure makes suppressed staphylococci, streptococci or enterococci important; a narrow fastidious-only approach can omit plausible causes.

questions.question: A stable adult with a prosthetic valve has a compatible subacute IE syndrome. Adequate pre-antibiotic cultures remain negative after 72 hours. No organism has been identified. Which next diagnostic strategy is most appropriate?
options: Broad-range bacterial PCR on blood without serological investigation
Extended routine-culture incubation without additional organism-directed tests
Laboratory review with Coxiella/Bartonella serology and directed molecular testing
Fungal biomarkers and repeat cultures without bacterial fastidious-organism testing
questions.explanation:
Escalating an Untreated Culture-Negative Investigation

Correct answer: Laboratory review with Coxiella/Bartonella serology and directed molecular testing

Expand Testing at About 72 Hours

**AHA 2025:** review persistent negative cultures with microbiology.

Check volume, antibiotic exposure, special culture requirements and selected extended incubation.

**Add Coxiella/Bartonella serology and directed molecular tests.**

Consider Brucella with relevant geography, animal contact or unpasteurized dairy exposure.

Use Complementary Evidence

**Exposure history guides testing:** animals, body lice, housing conditions, travel, surgery and implants.

Negative blood PCR may miss tissue-predominant infection; broad molecular tests can detect contaminants.

**Plan tissue culture, histology and PCR if surgery occurs.**

Do not delay treatment of HF, abscess or another source-control indication while awaiting send-away results.

Broad-range bacterial PCR on blood without serological investigation: Broad molecular methods can provide useful evidence in selected culture-negative cases. A negative blood assay may miss low-burden or tissue-predominant infection, so it should not replace the complementary serological and laboratory assessment.

Extended routine-culture incubation without additional organism-directed tests: Prolonged incubation can help recover selected slow-growing organisms and is worth discussing with microbiology. It does not address nonculturable causes adequately, so it is less complete than the coordinated serological and molecular evaluation.

Fungal biomarkers and repeat cultures without bacterial fastidious-organism testing: Fungal investigation is relevant with a compatible risk setting and prosthetic infection can be fungal. Restricting the evaluation to that pathway overlooks common fastidious BCNE causes that require specific serological or molecular methods.

AHA blood culture-negative endocarditis scientific statement, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.124.040218

questions.question: A livestock worker with pre-existing aortic-valve disease has months of constitutional symptoms, negative routine cultures and a small valve lesion. Phase-I C. burnetii IgG is 1:3200. Which cause is most strongly supported?
options: Tropheryma whipplei endocarditis
Bartonella henselae endocarditis
Brucella endocarditis
Coxiella burnetii endocarditis
questions.explanation:
Coxiella Endocarditis With a Subtle Valve Lesion

Correct answer: Coxiella burnetii endocarditis

Persistent Focal Q Fever

**Valve or vascular infection can be indolent and culture negative.**

Pre-existing valve disease and livestock exposure support investigation.

**Duke–ISCVID major threshold:** phase-I IgG ==>1:800==.

The 1:3200 result qualifies, but serology must accompany a compatible focal syndrome.

Prolonged Treatment and Monitoring

**CDC adult regimen:** doxycycline ==100 mg every 12 hours== plus hydroxychloroquine ==200 mg every 8 hours== for at least 18 months.

Prosthetic or difficult focal infection may require longer specialist-directed treatment; acute-Q-fever courses are insufficient.

**Follow clinical response, serology, interactions and retinal toxicity.**

One titre is not an automatic stopping rule; assess valve failure or uncontrolled infection for surgery and monitor relapse.

Tropheryma whipplei endocarditis: Whipple endocarditis can be indolent and culture negative, sometimes with preceding arthralgia. It requires appropriate molecular or tissue evidence and does not explain the stated Coxiella serological pattern as well.

Bartonella henselae endocarditis: Cat or flea exposure and compatible Bartonella serology or PCR would support this cause. The supplied high phase-I Coxiella result with livestock exposure instead supports Q fever-associated infection.

Brucella endocarditis: Livestock exposure and unpasteurized dairy can also suggest Brucella, which warrants organism-specific evaluation in the appropriate epidemiology. Exposure overlap does not negate the specific high phase-I Coxiella evidence in the stem.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: An adult experiencing housing insecurity has chronic fever, a valve lesion and immune-complex glomerulonephritis. Routine cultures are negative. There is a history of body-lice infestation and no livestock exposure. Which targeted organism investigation is most strongly indicated?
options: Brucella serology as the sole targeted test
Coxiella burnetii phase-I serology as the sole targeted test
Bartonella quintana serology and appropriate blood or tissue PCR
Tropheryma whipplei PCR as the sole targeted test
questions.explanation:
Bartonella and Housing-Related Exposure

Correct answer: Bartonella quintana serology and appropriate blood or tissue PCR

Exposure and Confirmation

**B. quintana:** body lice; **B. henselae:** cats/kittens and fleas.

Either can cause culture-negative IE with immune-complex renal injury.

**Serology plus targeted blood/tissue PCR.**

Qualifying IgG ≥1:800 or blood nucleic-acid detection provides major evidence; cross-reactivity and negative blood-PCR sensitivity limit interpretation.

Treatment and Source Assessment

**AHA 2025:** doxycycline ==100 mg every 12 hours== for 12 weeks, with rifampin for the first 6 weeks.

Rifampin 300 mg every 12 hours is a recognized adult combination dose; NIH HIV guidance has separate continuation requirements.

**Monitor liver tests, interactions, renal disease and response.**

Aminoglycoside renal toxicity is particularly relevant with glomerulonephritis.

**Treat infestation and assess valve dysfunction/source control.**

Lice eradication or renal improvement alone does not establish cure of IE.

Brucella serology as the sole targeted test: Brucella testing is useful with endemic residence, animal exposure or unpasteurized dairy. The distinctive exposure supplied here is body lice, so a Brucella-only strategy is less well matched.

Coxiella burnetii phase-I serology as the sole targeted test: Coxiella is an important cause of BCNE and often belongs in a broader evaluation. Body-lice exposure particularly favors B. quintana; Coxiella testing alone would miss the strongest epidemiological lead.

Tropheryma whipplei PCR as the sole targeted test: Whipple infection may warrant testing with an indolent culture-negative valve syndrome and compatible systemic features. The body-lice history points more directly toward B. quintana and should not be ignored in selecting tests.

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.topic: Blood culture-negative disease and organism clues
questions.question: A middle-aged man has years of unexplained migratory arthralgia followed by weight loss, HF and a destructive aortic-valve lesion. Routine blood cultures remain negative despite adequate sampling before antibiotics. He has no diarrhea. Which additional investigation is particularly appropriate?
options: Bartonella serology without considering another fastidious organism
Targeted T. whipplei PCR, including valve tissue testing if available
Coxiella phase-II serology as the decisive endocarditis test
Repeat routine bacterial cultures as the only etiological investigation
questions.explanation:
Whipple Endocarditis Without Diarrhea

Correct answer: Targeted T. whipplei PCR, including valve tissue testing if available

Whipple Disease Without Diarrhea

**Migratory arthralgia can precede culture-negative valve disease.**

HF and regurgitation may dominate; absent malabsorption does not exclude infection.

**Targeted blood PCR; valve PCR/histology when available.**

Negative blood PCR does not exclude tissue-predominant disease; stool/saliva positivity may reflect carriage.

Keep Treatment Frameworks Separate

**ESC 2023:** doxycycline ==200 mg/day== plus hydroxychloroquine ==200–600 mg/day== for at least 18 months.

**AHA 2025:** initial 4-week IV phase, e.g. ceftriaxone ==2 g daily==, then ≥11 months of appropriate oral maintenance.

These are distinct approaches, not a combined schedule.

**Assess CNS involvement, relapse and drug/retinal toxicity.**

Evidence is limited; specialist selection and treatment of valve failure, including indicated surgery, remain essential.

Bartonella serology without considering another fastidious organism: Bartonella is a valid component of a BCNE investigation and can cause systemic manifestations. The prolonged arthralgia and valve phenotype also warrant specific consideration of T. whipplei; the absence of diarrhea does not remove that possibility.

Coxiella phase-II serology as the decisive endocarditis test: Coxiella belongs in a suitable BCNE evaluation, but the endocarditis serological major definition uses phase-I evidence. A phase-II-only approach neither applies that rule correctly nor addresses the Whipple-compatible phenotype.

Repeat routine bacterial cultures as the only etiological investigation: Repeat cultures can document a newly detectable conventional pathogen and remain useful when sampling is inadequate. They are insufficient as the only strategy for suspected T. whipplei, which requires nonroutine molecular or tissue investigation.

questions.explanationHtml:
Whipple Endocarditis Without Diarrhea

Correct answer: Targeted T. whipplei PCR, including valve tissue testing if available

Whipple Disease Without Diarrhea

  • Migratory arthralgia can precede culture-negative valve disease.
    • HF and regurgitation may dominate; absent malabsorption does not exclude infection.
  • Targeted blood PCR; valve PCR/histology when available.
    • Negative blood PCR does not exclude tissue-predominant disease; stool/saliva positivity may reflect carriage.

Keep Treatment Frameworks Separate

  • ESC 2023: doxycycline 200 mg/day plus hydroxychloroquine 200–600 mg/day for at least 18 months.
  • AHA 2025: initial 4-week IV phase, e.g. ceftriaxone 2 g daily, then ≥11 months of appropriate oral maintenance.
    • These are distinct approaches, not a combined schedule.
  • Assess CNS involvement, relapse and drug/retinal toxicity.
    • Evidence is limited; specialist selection and treatment of valve failure, including indicated surgery, remain essential.

Other Options

  • Bartonella serology without considering another fastidious organism: Bartonella is a valid component of a BCNE investigation and can cause systemic manifestations. The prolonged arthralgia and valve phenotype also warrant specific consideration of T. whipplei; the absence of diarrhea does not remove that possibility.
  • Coxiella phase-II serology as the decisive endocarditis test: Coxiella belongs in a suitable BCNE evaluation, but the endocarditis serological major definition uses phase-I evidence. A phase-II-only approach neither applies that rule correctly nor addresses the Whipple-compatible phenotype.
  • Repeat routine bacterial cultures as the only etiological investigation: Repeat cultures can document a newly detectable conventional pathogen and remain useful when sampling is inadequate. They are insufficient as the only strategy for suspected T. whipplei, which requires nonroutine molecular or tissue investigation.

References

  • Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023
  • AHA blood culture-negative endocarditis scientific statement, 2025
  • Tropheryma whipplei endocarditis: primary clinical series, 2013
  • ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023

questions.question: A patient with BCNE is undergoing indicated valve surgery. No organism has been identified. Which specimen plan best preserves the opportunity for etiological diagnosis?
options: Coordinate separate appropriate specimens for microbiology, histology and molecular testing before fixation
Place all excised tissue in formalin and request culture later if histology is inconclusive
Send only a surface swab for routine bacterial culture
Request histology only because preoperative antibiotics make every microbial test unhelpful
questions.explanation:
Preserving the Diagnostic Opportunity at Valve Surgery

Correct answer: Coordinate separate appropriate specimens for microbiology, histology and molecular testing before fixation

Allocate Tissue Before Fixation

**Coordinate surgery, microbiology and pathology in advance.**

Provide antibiotics, exposure history and suspected pathogens; label representative tissue/prosthetic material appropriately.

**Preserve unfixed sterile material for required microbial tests and a separate histology portion.**

Follow the receiving laboratory’s transport protocol; formalin prevents conventional viable-organism culture.

Interpret the Combined Results

**Culture:** organism and susceptibility; **histology:** active inflammation/mimics; **molecular tests:** organism evidence despite culture suppression.

Select fungal/mycobacterial tests or special stains by clinical probability.

**DNA can persist after treatment and contamination can mislead.**

An isolated skin-organism PCR signal without corroboration is not automatic pathological definite IE. Negative treated tissue culture does not erase convincing operative or histological evidence.

Place all excised tissue in formalin and request culture later if histology is inconclusive: Formalin preserves material for histopathology and some molecular methods can use fixed tissue. It prevents recovery of viable organisms for conventional culture, so fixing every specimen unnecessarily sacrifices complementary evidence.

Send only a surface swab for routine bacterial culture: A swab may be used in some sampling situations, but actual operative tissue is more informative for the complementary investigations required here. A routine swab alone does not preserve histology or the full molecular opportunity.

Request histology only because preoperative antibiotics make every microbial test unhelpful: Previous antibiotics reduce culture yield but do not make all tissue testing futile. Molecular methods and selected stains may identify a cause, and culture can still contribute when properly handled.

AHA blood culture-negative endocarditis scientific statement, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.124.040218

Duke–ISCVID diagnostic criteria, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad271

questions.question: A patient has native mitral-valve IE caused by a penicillin- and ceftriaxone-susceptible oral streptococcus. There is no abscess or surgical indication, but chronic kidney disease makes an aminoglycoside unattractive. Which definitive regimen is most appropriate?
options: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for four weeks
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for two weeks
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for six weeks
Vancomycin with exposure-guided dosing for four weeks
questions.explanation:
A Full Beta-Lactam Course for Susceptible Oral Streptococci

Correct answer: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for four weeks

Full Beta-Lactam Course

**Susceptible oral-streptococcal NVE:** ceftriaxone ==2 g IV every 24 hours for 4 weeks==.

Susceptible PVE ordinarily requires 6 weeks; suitable penicillin/amoxicillin regimens are alternatives.

**Two-week monotherapy is not the short-course strategy.**

Selected abbreviated treatment requires a synergistic combination and strict eligibility.

Renal Risk and Follow-Up

**CKD favors avoiding unnecessary aminoglycoside exposure.**

Monitor cultures, blood counts, organ function and ceftriaxone adverse effects, including biliary complications.

**Reassess anatomy throughout treatment.**

Abscess, embolic complications or valve failure change management; susceptibility alone does not establish uncomplicated disease.

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for two weeks: The two-week streptococcal approach is a selected synergistic combination regimen, not a two-week ceftriaxone monotherapy course. The renal context also argues against using an aminoglycoside merely to shorten treatment.

Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours for six weeks: A six-week beta-lactam course is standard for susceptible oral-streptococcal PVE and may be needed in some complicated settings. The supplied uncomplicated native-valve setting supports the four-week monotherapy course.

Vancomycin with exposure-guided dosing for four weeks: Vancomycin is an alternative when a suitable beta-lactam cannot be used, such as a relevant serious allergy. No such limitation is supplied, and it adds avoidable renal monitoring concerns when ceftriaxone is active and suitable.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

AHA adult infective endocarditis scientific statement, 2015 — https://www.idsociety.org/globalassets/idsa/practice-guidelines/infective-endocarditis-in-adults-diagnosis-antimicrobial-therapy-and-management-of-complications.pdf

questions.question: An adult has uncomplicated oral-streptococcal native-valve IE with amoxicillin MIC 1 mg/L and ceftriaxone MIC 0.25 mg/L. Renal toxicity is a concern and ceftriaxone is tolerated. Which strategy follows the SPILF–AEPEI position statement published in 2025?
options: A full ceftriaxone course with gentamicin required by the amoxicillin result alone
A two-week ceftriaxone monotherapy course
A full ceftriaxone course without obligatory adjunctive gentamicin
A full vancomycin course despite a suitable active beta-lactam
questions.explanation:
Drug-Specific MICs in Streptococcal Endocarditis

Correct answer: A full ceftriaxone course without obligatory adjunctive gentamicin

SPILF–AEPEI Regimen Selection

**Use the MIC of the beta-lactam selected for treatment.**

Ceftriaxone MIC ≤0.5 mg/L supports monotherapy in this framework despite reduced amoxicillin susceptibility.

**Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily for 4 weeks** for the supplied uncomplicated NVE.

PVE requires 6 weeks; complications may change the plan.

Why the Framework Matters

**This position differs from older routine aminoglycoside-combination rules.**

Gentamicin toxicity should not be incurred solely because another beta-lactam has a higher MIC.

**Do not generalize to ceftriaxone-resistant isolates or a 2-week monotherapy course.**

Assess both susceptibility results, allergy, cultures and anatomy.

A full ceftriaxone course with gentamicin required by the amoxicillin result alone: Some guideline regimens add gentamicin for reduced beta-lactam susceptibility. SPILF–AEPEI permits an adequate monotherapy course when the selected ceftriaxone itself is susceptible.

A two-week ceftriaxone monotherapy course: The selected short streptococcal course is not a two-week ceftriaxone-alone strategy. The newer monotherapy position concerns an adequate full course, not arbitrary shortening.

A full vancomycin course despite a suitable active beta-lactam: Vancomycin has a role when resistance or allergy prevents a suitable beta-lactam. The stem provides ceftriaxone susceptibility without such a limitation, so vancomycin is not required and can add renal monitoring concerns.

SPILF–AEPEI antibiotic therapy position statement, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.idnow.2024.105011

questions.question: Which patient is the best candidate for a two-week beta-lactam–gentamicin regimen for susceptible oral-streptococcal IE?
options: An adult with a prosthetic valve and rapidly cleared bacteremia
An adult with uncomplicated native-valve disease and normal renal function
An adult with native-valve disease and an undrained splenic abscess
An adult with uncomplicated native-valve disease and substantial chronic renal impairment
questions.explanation:
Eligibility for Two-Week Streptococcal Therapy

Correct answer: An adult with uncomplicated native-valve disease and normal renal function

Short-Course Eligibility

**Susceptible oral streptococcus + uncomplicated NVE + normal renal function.**

Exclude prosthetic infection, local invasion and important extracardiac complications.

**Example 2-week combination:** ceftriaxone ==2 g IV daily== plus gentamicin ==3 mg/kg/day==, commonly once daily.

Individualize aminoglycoside dosing to weight, clearance and drug concentrations.

Safety and Alternatives

**Monitor renal, auditory and vestibular toxicity.**

Rapid defervescence alone does not establish eligibility.

**Four-week active beta-lactam monotherapy** is a standard alternative.

Do not extend the short-course rule to enterococci, staphylococci or nutritionally variant streptococci; outpatient treatment requires stability and reliable monitoring.

An adult with a prosthetic valve and rapidly cleared bacteremia: Rapid clearance is reassuring but does not convert prosthetic infection into the selected short-course native-valve population. Susceptible oral-streptococcal PVE ordinarily requires a longer course.

An adult with native-valve disease and an undrained splenic abscess: The organism may be susceptible, but an abscess makes the episode complicated and introduces a source-control problem. The two-week uncomplicated-IE approach cannot be selected on susceptibility alone.

An adult with uncomplicated native-valve disease and substantial chronic renal impairment: Native-valve anatomy alone is insufficient for eligibility. Aminoglycoside toxicity is a major concern with renal impairment, and a full suitable beta-lactam course avoids forcing a nephrotoxic short-course strategy.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

AHA adult infective endocarditis scientific statement, 2015 — https://www.idsociety.org/globalassets/idsa/practice-guidelines/infective-endocarditis-in-adults-diagnosis-antimicrobial-therapy-and-management-of-complications.pdf

questions.question: A patient with left-sided native-valve IE was started empirically on vancomycin. Cultures identify MSSA. Renal function is normal, and there is no relevant beta-lactam allergy. Which definitive treatment choice is preferred?
options: Continued vancomycin as the sole definitive agent
An IV antistaphylococcal penicillin or cefazolin
Cefazolin with gentamicin for the initial two weeks
Cefazolin with rifampin for the full course
questions.explanation:
Definitive Therapy for MSSA Native-Valve Infection

Correct answer: An IV antistaphylococcal penicillin or cefazolin

Target MSSA With a Beta-Lactam

**Normal-renal-function adult examples:** cloxacillin/oxacillin ==2 g IV every 4 hours== or cefazolin ==2 g IV every 8 hours==.

Select by allergy phenotype, availability and organ function; renal impairment changes cefazolin dosing.

**Left-sided staphylococcal NVE:** usually 4–6 weeks.

The restricted short-course right-sided pathway does not apply.

Adjuncts and Monitoring

**Routine gentamicin or rifampin is not indicated in this native-valve setting.**

Do not import foreign-material or streptococcal synergy rules.

**Monitor blood counts, renal/hepatic function and cultures.**

Penicillins can cause interstitial nephritis, hepatic injury, electrolyte disturbance and cytopenias.

**Persistent bacteremia requires source reassessment**, including metastatic infection and surgical indications.

Continued vancomycin as the sole definitive agent: Vancomycin is useful for MRSA or when a suitable beta-lactam cannot be given. For a beta-lactam-tolerant patient with MSSA, a targeted antistaphylococcal beta-lactam is preferred rather than retaining empirical MRSA coverage.

Cefazolin with gentamicin for the initial two weeks: Cefazolin is an appropriate MSSA agent, but adding gentamicin in staphylococcal NVE has not shown a clinical benefit that justifies its renal toxicity. The aminoglycoside rules from selected streptococcal or enterococcal regimens should not be transferred here.

Cefazolin with rifampin for the full course: Rifampin has a selected foreign-material role in staphylococcal infection and substantial interaction and resistance concerns. The stem describes native-valve disease without such material, so routine addition is not justified.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

AHA adult infective endocarditis scientific statement, 2015 — https://www.idsociety.org/globalassets/idsa/practice-guidelines/infective-endocarditis-in-adults-diagnosis-antimicrobial-therapy-and-management-of-complications.pdf
