questions.question: A pacemaker generator has eroded through the skin, with a small draining sinus. The patient is afebrile, blood cultures are negative and echocardiography shows no vegetation. Extraction risk is acceptable. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Arrange complete system removal with appropriate antimicrobial treatment and reassessment of pacing needs
Treat with antibiotics while retaining the system because blood cultures are negative
Remove the generator and retain the transvenous leads because no vegetation is seen
Revise the pocket and close the skin after local debridement
questions.explanation:
Pacemaker Pocket Erosion and Definite Device Infection

Correct answer: Arrange complete system removal with appropriate antimicrobial treatment and reassessment of pacing needs

Definite Pocket Infection

**Exposed generator, sinus or purulence establishes pocket infection.**

Negative blood cultures and absent vegetations do not exclude it.

**Superficial incisional infection** has no pocket communication and may permit hardware retention.

Source Control

**Complete system removal plus antimicrobials** is the standard when extraction is feasible.

Retained leads can sustain biofilm; generator-only removal is inadequate.

**Isolated uncomplicated pocket infection:** commonly ==10–14 days== after removal.

Systemic or valve infection requires a longer organism-specific course.

**Reassess pacing need and dependence.**

Arrange temporary support if needed; reimplant at an appropriate different site after infection control.

Treat with antibiotics while retaining the system because blood cultures are negative: Antibiotics with retained hardware may be used in exceptional patients who cannot undergo extraction, but exposed hardware establishes contamination and definite pocket infection. Negative blood cultures do not make retention the standard curative approach.

Remove the generator and retain the transvenous leads because no vegetation is seen: A vegetation need not be visible for the system to be infected. Retained leads can sustain biofilm and relapse, so isolated generator removal is inadequate for definite pocket infection when complete removal is feasible.

Revise the pocket and close the skin after local debridement: Pocket revision may address selected noninfectious mechanical problems before exposure. Established erosion with a draining sinus represents infection, and closure over retained contaminated hardware does not provide reliable source control.

questions.question: A patient with a pacemaker has persistent S. aureus bacteremia and a lead vegetation. Extraction is technically feasible after specialist assessment. Which definitive strategy is most appropriate?
options: Complete generator and lead removal with active antimicrobial therapy
A prolonged antibiotic course while retaining the entire system
Remove the generator but retain the infected transvenous lead
Exchange the generator immediately into the same pocket during treatment
questions.explanation:
Source Control for Confirmed Lead Infection

Correct answer: Complete generator and lead removal with active antimicrobial therapy

Remove the Infected Reservoir

**Confirmed lead infection requires complete-system extraction when feasible.**

Antibiotics may suppress bloodstream growth without sterilizing biofilm.

**Use an experienced extraction team with rescue capability.**

Lead age, anatomy, vegetation burden and valve-surgery needs influence approach.

Treatment After Extraction

**Continue pathogen-directed therapy and clearance cultures.**

Duration follows organism, bacteremia, lead/valve involvement and complications; investigate metastatic sites.

**Retention/suppression is an exception for genuinely prohibitive removal risk.**

Transient improvement does not establish cure with retained infected hardware.

**Reassess permanent-device need; bridge rhythm support if required.**

Reimplant at a suitable distant site after clinical and microbiological control.

A prolonged antibiotic course while retaining the entire system: Device retention may be considered when removal is genuinely impossible or prohibitive, often with an individualized suppressive plan. It is inferior source control for confirmed lead infection when extraction is feasible.

Remove the generator but retain the infected transvenous lead: Generator removal alone does not eliminate an infected lead or its biofilm. Complete infected-system removal is the standard objective, with specialist planning for the extraction risks.

Exchange the generator immediately into the same pocket during treatment: Immediate replacement leaves the contaminated site and potentially infected leads in place. Reimplantation requires separate assessment of need, location and infection control rather than a same-pocket exchange.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

EHRA international CIED-infection consensus, 2020 — https://academic.oup.com/ejcts/article/57/1/e1/5625578

questions.question: A patient with a CIED has persistent S. aureus bacteremia without another identified focus. The pocket appears normal and an initial TEE shows no vegetation. Which diagnostic plan is most appropriate?
options: Replace the generator diagnostically while leaving the leads in place
Exclude CIED infection because the pocket is clinically normal
Classify the episode as uncomplicated solely from the negative TEE
Continue CIED and valve assessment with repeat or complementary imaging and source review
questions.explanation:
A Negative Initial Lead Study Does Not End the Assessment

Correct answer: Continue CIED and valve assessment with repeat or complementary imaging and source review

Negative TEE Does Not Exclude CIED Infection

**Persistent S. aureus bacteremia remains concerning despite a normal pocket.**

Small/early lesions or extracardiac lead involvement may escape visualization.

**Repeat cultures and review vascular access, device history and other sources.**

CRP or fever improvement does not establish clearance.

Resolve the Remaining Suspicion

**Repeat echo and selected FDG-PET/CT can complement the first study.**

Negative PET does not universally exclude lead infection; a lead mass can also be noninfectious.

**Consider extraction when confirmed infection or compelling unexplained persistence supports it.**

Integrate pathogen, alternative sources and procedural risk rather than requiring a visible vegetation.

**Generator exchange is not a diagnostic substitute.**

Replace the generator diagnostically while leaving the leads in place: A generator exchange is not a diagnostic substitute for evaluation of the bloodstream source. It can add procedural risk while retaining infected lead material if infection is present.

Exclude CIED infection because the pocket is clinically normal: Hematogenous lead or valve infection can occur without pocket inflammation. A normal pocket does not resolve unexplained persistent S. aureus bacteremia.

Classify the episode as uncomplicated solely from the negative TEE: An early or technically limited study can miss disease, and persistent bacteremia argues against an uncomplicated designation. Clearance, source assessment and relevant complications still need evaluation.

questions.question: A CIED has been completely removed for lead infection with a documented vegetation. The patient still requires a permanent device but has a safe temporary pacing bridge. Under ESC 2023, which reimplantation plan is most appropriate?
options: Use the original pocket once the first post-extraction culture is negative
Use a distant site after clinical resolution and at least two weeks of negative blood cultures
Use a distant site after seventy-two hours of negative cultures without considering the vegetation
Reimplant immediately because complete extraction removes any need to document clearance
questions.explanation:
Reimplantation After CIED Infection With Vegetations

Correct answer: Use a distant site after clinical resolution and at least two weeks of negative blood cultures

Reassess Need and Bridge Safely

**Confirm the ongoing permanent-device indication.**

Use appropriate temporary support if necessary; select a distant replacement site and suitable platform.

ESC 2023 Clearance Intervals

**Visible vegetation:** infection signs resolved plus ≥2 weeks of negative cultures.

Without vegetations or relevant residual ghosts, the usual minimum framework is ≥72 hours of negative cultures after extraction.

**Reimplant as late as practical**, not automatically on the earliest qualifying day.

Persistent valve/metastatic infection can require further delay.

**Monitor the temporary system and complete antimicrobials.**

Count documented microbiological clearance, not simply time since extraction.

Use the original pocket once the first post-extraction culture is negative: A single negative culture is not sufficient evidence of sustained control, and the previous infected pocket is not the preferred replacement site. The documented vegetation calls for a longer clearance interval.

Use a distant site after seventy-two hours of negative cultures without considering the vegetation: The seventy-two-hour interval applies to the appropriate no-vegetation or ghost-free setting once signs resolve. The stem specifically supplies a vegetation, for which ESC recommends at least two weeks of negative cultures.

Reimplant immediately because complete extraction removes any need to document clearance: Extraction removes a source but does not prove that bacteremia or other infection has resolved. Reimplantation during active infection risks contaminating the new system.

questions.question: Blood cultures clear in a patient with prosthetic-valve IE, but severe regurgitation, periannular extension and worsening renal function remain. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Declining inflammatory markers can substitute for follow-up imaging of the valve
Culture clearance removes the need for inpatient risk assessment if the patient is afebrile
The organism alone determines prognosis once repeat cultures are negative
Microbiological improvement does not remove the high risk from structural and organ complications
questions.explanation:
Risk Assessment After Bloodstream Clearance

Correct answer: Microbiological improvement does not remove the high risk from structural and organ complications

Integrate Risk Domains

**Assess host, pathogen, anatomy and organ function together.**

HF, prosthetic involvement, invasive infection, persistent bacteremia, renal failure and neurological complications are adverse features.

**Reassess dynamically.**

One improved variable does not negate deterioration in another domain.

Link Risk to Action

**Escalate Endocarditis Team and surgical assessment when indicated.**

Use imaging, perfusion, rhythm, renal trends and microbiology to define the unresolved problem.

**Avoid a universal individual mortality estimate from cohort averages.**

Counsel according to recoverability, complications and treatment options; continue follow-up after discharge.

Declining inflammatory markers can substitute for follow-up imaging of the valve: Markers track inflammation imperfectly and cannot show whether regurgitation or periannular destruction has resolved; anatomical reassessment remains necessary.

Culture clearance removes the need for inpatient risk assessment if the patient is afebrile: Clearance is favorable but does not resolve severe valve dysfunction, invasive anatomy or renal injury; these findings still need urgent integrated assessment.

The organism alone determines prognosis once repeat cultures are negative: Pathogen matters, but hemodynamics, prosthetic involvement, extension, neurological injury and organ dysfunction independently influence risk and treatment.

ESC endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: Which patient–procedure combination clearly warrants dental IE prophylaxis under current AHA guidance?
options: A patient with a prosthetic valve undergoing routine dental radiography
A patient with an isolated bicuspid aortic valve undergoing dental extraction
A patient with a pacemaker undergoing routine dental extraction
A patient with a prosthetic valve undergoing dental extraction
questions.explanation:
Dental Prophylaxis: Cardiac Risk and Procedure Together

Correct answer: A patient with a prosthetic valve undergoing dental extraction

Require Both Cardiac and Procedural Eligibility

**High-risk cardiac condition + gingival/periapical manipulation or oral-mucosal perforation.**

A prosthetic valve with dental extraction satisfies both; radiography does not meet the procedural criterion.

**Cardiac groups are listed in the table.**

Prosthetic valves include transcatheter valves; pacemaker, isolated bicuspid valve or MVP alone does not qualify.

Prevention Beyond the Dose

**Use the recommended single dose after allergy review.**

Verify the exact congenital/transplant lesion rather than relying on its broad label.

**Maintain oral hygiene and regular dental care.**

Procedural prophylaxis does not prevent all IE or replace management of other sources; document both eligibility components.

AHA cardiac group | Qualifying examples

Prosthesis or repair material | Prosthetic valve; valve-repair ring, chord or clip

Previous infection | Prior IE

Selected CHD | Unrepaired cyanotic CHD; repaired CHD with residual shunt or regurgitation at or adjacent to prosthetic material

Cardiac transplant | Valve regurgitation from a structurally abnormal valve

A patient with a prosthetic valve undergoing routine dental radiography: The cardiac condition is high risk, but the procedure does not involve the qualifying gingival or periapical manipulation or oral mucosal perforation. The cardiac and procedural conditions must both be satisfied.

A patient with an isolated bicuspid aortic valve undergoing dental extraction: Bicuspid disease increases IE risk but does not alone place the patient in the AHA high-risk prophylaxis group. Good oral care remains important; the broader epidemiological risk does not automatically create prophylaxis eligibility.

A patient with a pacemaker undergoing routine dental extraction: A pacemaker alone is not a cardiac indication for dental IE prophylaxis. Device-implantation prophylaxis is a separate situation and must not be transferred to later dental care.

AHA prevention of IE wallet card, current guidance — https://www.heart.org/-/media/files/health-topics/infective-endocarditis/infective-endocarditis-wallet-card.pdf

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: An adult with a previous IE episode is scheduled for a qualifying dental procedure, can take oral medicines and has no penicillin allergy. Which planned regimen follows current AHA guidance?
options: Amoxicillin 2 g orally only after completion of the procedure
Amoxicillin 500 mg orally once, thirty to sixty minutes before the procedure
Amoxicillin 2 g orally once, thirty to sixty minutes before the procedure
Amoxicillin 2 g before the procedure followed by scheduled doses for three days
questions.explanation:
Adult Amoxicillin Dental Prophylaxis

Correct answer: Amoxicillin 2 g orally once, thirty to sixty minutes before the procedure

Single Planned Dose

**Amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 minutes before** the qualifying procedure.

If inadvertently missed, a dose within 2 hours afterward is a rescue provision, not preferred planned timing.

**Prophylaxis differs from treating dental infection.**

Routine multiday dosing is unnecessary.

Route and Allergy Alternatives

**Use the table to choose the single adult dose.**

Clarify the reaction history; avoid specified cephalosporin options after penicillin-associated anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria.

**Clindamycin is no longer recommended** for dental IE prophylaxis.

Review macrolide interactions and other patient factors; provide clear timing instructions and ongoing oral-care advice.

Adult situation | Single dose thirty to sixty minutes before

Oral, no penicillin allergy | Amoxicillin ==2 g==

Unable to take oral medicine | Ampicillin ==2 g== IM/IV; or cefazolin/ceftriaxone ==1 g== IM/IV

Oral penicillin-allergy alternatives | Cephalexin ==2 g==; azithromycin/clarithromycin ==500 mg==; or doxycycline ==100 mg==

Immediate penicillin hypersensitivity | Avoid cephalosporin options specified as unsuitable in AHA guidance; select a suitable non-beta-lactam alternative

Amoxicillin 2 g orally only after completion of the procedure: A missed pre-procedure dose can be addressed under the guidance’s post-procedure rescue provision. For a planned procedure with dosing available, the recommended timing is before the bacteremia-producing intervention.

Amoxicillin 500 mg orally once, thirty to sixty minutes before the procedure: A 500 mg dose appears in treatment schedules for other infections, but it is below the recommended single adult prophylaxis dose. Do not substitute a familiar therapeutic tablet strength for the specified regimen.

Amoxicillin 2 g before the procedure followed by scheduled doses for three days: Longer amoxicillin treatment is appropriate for an actual infection when indicated. Routine dental IE prophylaxis is a single-dose strategy, not an additional multiday therapeutic course.

AHA prevention of IE wallet card, current guidance — https://www.heart.org/-/media/files/health-topics/infective-endocarditis/infective-endocarditis-wallet-card.pdf

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic valve is scheduled for elective colonoscopy without active infection. Which statement accurately distinguishes current AHA advice from ESC 2023?
options: Both societies recommend prophylaxis for this prosthetic-valve colonoscopy
AHA does not recommend IE prophylaxis here; ESC allows consideration for selected high-risk nondental procedures
AHA permits consideration here; ESC advises against it
Both societies advise against prophylaxis in this nondental setting
questions.explanation:
AHA and ESC Positions on Nondental Prophylaxis

Correct answer: AHA does not recommend IE prophylaxis here; ESC allows consideration for selected high-risk nondental procedures

Named Guideline Difference

**AHA:** no IE prophylaxis for elective colonoscopy without active infection solely because of a prosthetic valve.

The same principle covers TEE, GI endoscopy and cystoscopy in that setting.

**ESC 2023:** prophylaxis may be considered for selected high-risk invasive nondental procedures.

Class IIb with limited evidence; not a universal mandate or proven randomized benefit.

Keep Separate Indications Separate

**Active infection requires treatment and procedure-specific assessment.**

Other procedural prophylaxis indications can exist independently of IE prevention.

**Document the society/framework and individualized rationale.**

Do not combine conflicting recommendations into an unnamed rule; retain asepsis, oral/skin care and prompt fever evaluation.

Both societies recommend prophylaxis for this prosthetic-valve colonoscopy: AHA specifically does not recommend IE prophylaxis for nondental procedures without active infection. ESC’s selected high-risk nondental recommendation is discretionary, not a universal mandate.

AHA permits consideration here; ESC advises against it: This reverses the relevant guidance difference. ESC moved to a may-be-considered position for selected high-risk settings, while AHA retains the no-routine-prophylaxis approach in the supplied scenario.

Both societies advise against prophylaxis in this nondental setting: That position reflects the AHA approach here and older more restrictive European advice. ESC 2023 instead permits consideration in selected high-risk invasive nondental procedures, so the blanket comparison misses the update.

questions.question: A patient has completed treatment for S. gallolyticus IE and is clinically improving. No recent adequate colon evaluation is documented. Which follow-up plan is most appropriate?
options: Arrange appropriate colon evaluation and structured cardiac, microbiological and prevention follow-up
Omit colon evaluation because a routine abdominal CT showed no mass
Investigate the colon only if overt lower-GI bleeding develops
End follow-up after the final antibiotic dose if fever has resolved
questions.explanation:
Follow-Up After Streptococcus gallolyticus IE

Correct answer: Arrange appropriate colon evaluation and structured cardiac, microbiological and prevention follow-up

Investigate Colorectal Pathology

**S. gallolyticus IE warrants appropriate colon evaluation.**

Lesions may be silent; routine abdominal CT does not replace mucosal assessment.

**Review prior colonoscopy quality and timing.**

Coordinate with recovery, cardiac stability and anticoagulation needs.

Post-Treatment Follow-Up

**Establish clinical/echo baseline and arrange review.**

Follow residual valve disease and HF; obtain post-treatment cultures as appropriate and investigate new fever promptly.

**Relapse suggests persistent infection; reinfection may involve new exposure or organisms.**

Interpret timing and microbiology together; reinforce dental/skin care and future prophylaxis eligibility.

**Observational studies support considering colon evaluation in E. faecalis IE**, including cases with an identified source.

This association does not establish a universal screening mandate for every enterococcal bacteremia; individualize the evaluation.

Omit colon evaluation because a routine abdominal CT showed no mass: CT may identify major pathology but does not replace an appropriate assessment of mucosal colorectal disease in this organism-associated setting. A negative routine scan is not sufficient reason to omit colon evaluation.

Investigate the colon only if overt lower-GI bleeding develops: Colorectal lesions associated with S. gallolyticus can be clinically silent. Waiting for bleeding misses the reason for organism-directed investigation.

End follow-up after the final antibiotic dose if fever has resolved: Defervescence is reassuring but does not address residual valve dysfunction, relapse, reinfection or the relevant portal of entry. Structured follow-up remains necessary after the antimicrobial course.

ESC infective endocarditis guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad193

Multicenter observational study of colorectal disease in E. faecalis IE, 2020 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31444092/
